lesson.title: How Good Is 'Common' Rejection? Quantifying CMRR
lesson.summary: The common-mode rejection ratio is a single decibel number that expresses how much more strongly a difference amplifier responds to genuine differential signals than to unwanted signals appearing equally on both inputs.
lesson.body:
The ideal difference amplifier assumes perfectly matched resistors and produces exactly zero output when both inputs carry the same voltage. Real resistors have tolerance, and real op-amps have their own imperfections, so that cancellation is never quite perfect. A real circuit ends up with a small but nonzero common-mode gain, Acm, on top of the intended differential gain, Ad.

CMRR is defined as the ratio of these two gains, Ad divided by Acm, and it is almost always expressed logarithmically using the same decibel definition covered earlier: CMRR in dB = 20 times log10(Ad / Acm). The factor of 20, rather than 10, is used here because Ad and Acm are both voltage gains, the same voltage form of the decibel used throughout this unit.

Continue the difference amplifier example from earlier, where Ad = 10. Suppose careful bench measurement shows that applying a 1V signal to both inputs at once (V1 = V2 = 1V, pure common mode) produces a measured output of 10mV instead of the ideal 0V. That means Acm = 10mV / 1V = 0.01, using the same "output per volt of input" definition as Ad. Then Ad / Acm = 10 / 0.01 = 1000. Since 10 cubed is 1000, log10(1000) = 3 exactly, so CMRR = 20 times 3 = 60dB.

For context, plain resistor-based difference amplifiers typically land somewhere around 50 to 70dB, limited mostly by resistor tolerance. Instrumentation amplifiers, thanks to the buffered, symmetric input stage covered earlier, routinely reach 80 to 120dB. A higher CMRR always means less unwanted common-mode signal reaches the output relative to the wanted differential signal, a distinction that becomes very concrete in a real, noisy environment, the subject of the next concept.
